title: A 'Good Ear' Makes Language Learning Easier — Study
paragraphs: Language education often includes a lot of grammar rules, reading and writing. All of these have value, but a new study has found that focusing on how a language sounds may actually make learning easier.

The study, published in The Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, shows that people who are better at noticing fine details in sounds may be better — and faster — at learning the pronunciation of new languages.
This skill is called "auditory precision," but it may also be described as having a "good ear."
For the study, researchers from University College London and Tohoku University in the city of Sendai worked with 67 English language learners in Japan.

They first measured the learners' ability to pick up on small differences in non-speech sounds. They then scanned the participants' brains while they tried to distinguish differences between English vowel sounds.
For example, the learners listened for the differences between the "a" sound in "cat" and the "uh" in cup — two vowel sounds that don't match directly with Japanese vowels.
In another similar task, participants listened for differences between similar non-speech sounds.
The results showed that during the listening tasks, learners with a "good ear" relied far less on the brain's left sensorimotor system — part of the brain heavily involved in language processing.
While it may seem like that should be a negative for language learning, their brains treating the new sounds like they weren't speech actually let them bypass their own first language filters.
With less interference from the patterns of their own language, it was easier for these learners to accurately process the new sounds.
The good news for all language learners is that you can improve your auditory precision skills — in other words, get a "good ear" — through practice.
The research team hopes to use its findings to develop a new form of language and auditory training for language learners.
